```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(plotly)

# All data come from the analysis repository
base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income/main/"

panel    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "data/processed/panel.csv"))
by_year  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/preston_by_year.csv"))
shift    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/curve_shift.csv"))
covid    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/covid_by_income.csv"))
outliers <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/outliers.csv"))
key      <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/key_stats.csv"))
sens     <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/sensitivity.csv"))

# Helpers for inline numbers
ks  <- function(stat) key$value[key$stat == stat]
num <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
grp <- function(g, col) covid[[col]][covid$income_group == g]

# One row per World Bank region: raw name, short label, colour
region_table <- tibble(
  region = c("East Asia & Pacific", "Europe & Central Asia",
             "Latin America & Caribbean",
             "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan",
             "North America", "South Asia", "Sub-Saharan Africa"),
  region_short = c("East Asia & Pacific", "Europe & Central Asia",
                   "Latin America & Caribbean", "Middle East & North Africa",
                   "North America", "South Asia", "Sub-Saharan Africa"),
  color = c("#2b8cbe", "#7b3294", "#e6550d", "#a6761d",
            "#31a354", "#756bb1", "#c51b8a")
)
region_colors <- setNames(region_table$color, region_table$region_short)
```

## The question

Every government publishes a GDP per capita number and a life expectancy number,
but the two are almost never read against each other across countries. Read
together, they produce a price. The **Preston curve** plots life expectancy
against log GDP per capita for all countries in a given year, and its slope
answers a plain question: *if a country's income doubles, how many more years
of life does it buy?*

Two things make the curve worth watching over time. First, the slope has been
strikingly stable: about 4.7 years of life per doubling of income for three
decades. Stability turns the curve into a measuring instrument, because if the
price of income is roughly constant, then any movement of the whole curve is a
change in the *technology of survival* — medicine, sanitation, nutrition,
vaccination — that income does not capture. Second, the curve has been moving,
and it has been moving faster at the bottom of the income distribution than at
the top.

## Data and method

The data come from the [World Bank Indicators API](https://api.worldbank.org/v2)
(CC BY 4.0), three indicators for every country from 1990 to 2023: life
expectancy at birth (`SP.DYN.LE00.IN`), GDP per capita at PPP in constant 2021
international dollars (`NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD`), and population (`SP.POP.TOTL`).
The panel keeps `r n_distinct(panel$country_iso3)` countries over
`r min(panel$year)`–`r max(panel$year)` (`r format(nrow(panel), big.mark = ",")`
country-years) after dropping World Bank aggregates, country-years missing any
indicator, and countries with fewer than one million inhabitants, whose life
expectancy is estimated from small numbers and swings wildly between years.

The method is deliberately simple. Life expectancy is regressed on
log2(GDP per capita) separately in each year; the slope is the price of income.
The fitted curve is then read off at \$5,000 and \$40,000 to measure how it moved
over time. For the pandemic, each country's actual 2019–2021 change is compared
with its own 2010–2019 pace, annualised and projected across the two pandemic
years, so that the comparison is not contaminated by the two windows having
different lengths.

## 1. What an extra dollar buys

Fitting the curve year by year gives a median slope of
`r num(ks("median_slope_by_year"))` years of life per doubling of income, and
`r num(ks("pooled_slope"))` in a pooled model with year effects. The fit is
good — R² runs from `r num(by_year$r_squared[by_year$year == 1990])` in 1990 to
`r num(by_year$r_squared[by_year$year == 2023])` in 2023 — so income explains
most, but far from all, of the cross-country spread in life expectancy.

The residual is the interesting part. Around the line sit countries that reach
far more, or far less, life expectancy than their income predicts: not
necessarily rich or poor countries, but countries whose health outcomes are out
of line with their material circumstances.

## 2. The curve moved up, and moved up more for the poor

Reading the fitted curve at two reference incomes shows how much the whole
relationship shifted between 1990 and 2019.

```{r}
#| label: shift-table
shift |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2005, 2019, 2021, 2023)) |>
  transmute(
    Year = year,
    `At $5,000`  = sprintf("%+.2f", shift_5k_vs_1990),
    `At $40,000` = sprintf("%+.2f", shift_40k_vs_1990)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

A country at \$5,000 per capita in 2019 would have been expected to live about
`r num(ks("shift_5k_1990_to_2019"))` years *less* than the 1990 curve predicted
for that income; at \$40,000 the gap is `r num(ks("shift_40k_1990_to_2019"))`
years. The curve did not shift up uniformly. It shifted up more at the bottom,
which is the signature of improvements that matter most where health starts from
a low base: the disease environment improved for everyone, and poorer countries
had more to gain from it.

## 3. The interactive view: the curve, one year at a time

A static scatter plot of the 2019 cross-section answers one question — where do
countries sit relative to income *this year* — and answers it well. It is close
to useless for the question I actually care about, which is how the
relationship *moves*. So the main figure below is an interactive one: the
cross-section is animated from 1990 to 2023, with the fitted curve re-drawn for
every year.

```{r}
#| label: interactive-preston
#| fig-height: 7.3

hover_text <- panel |>
  left_join(region_table, by = "region") |>
  mutate(
    marker_size = 4 + 36 * sqrt(population / max(population)),
    label = paste0("<b>", country_name, "</b><br>",
                   "Year: ", year, "<br>",
                   "Life expectancy: ", round(life_expectancy, 1), " years<br>",
                   "GDP per capita: $", format(round(gdp_per_capita), big.mark = ","), "<br>",
                   "Population: ", format(round(population / 1e6), big.mark = ","), " million<br>",
                   "Region: ", region_short, "<br>",
                   "Income group: ", income_group)
  )

curve_all <- by_year |>
  filter(!is.na(slope)) |>
  select(year, intercept, slope) |>
  crossing(gdp_per_capita = exp(seq(log(1500), log(150000), length.out = 100))) |>
  mutate(predicted = intercept + slope * log2(gdp_per_capita))

plot_ly(
  data = hover_text,
  x = ~gdp_per_capita, y = ~life_expectancy,
  color = ~region_short, frame = ~year,
  text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text",
  type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
  marker = list(size = hover_text$marker_size, opacity = 0.65, sizemin = 3,
                line = list(width = 0.4, color = "white")),
  colors = region_colors
) |>
  add_trace(
    data = curve_all, x = ~gdp_per_capita, y = ~predicted, frame = ~year,
    inherit = FALSE,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = "black", width = 1.4, dash = "dot"),
    hoverinfo = "none", showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "", type = "log", range = c(log10(1500), log10(150000)),
                 tickvals = c(2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000),
                 ticktext = c("$2k", "$5k", "$10k", "$20k", "$50k", "$100k")),
    yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy at birth (years)", range = c(38, 90)),
    title = list(
      text = "The health-income curve, one year at a time<br><sup>Drag the slider or press play to step through 1990–2023</sup>",
      font = list(size = 16)
    ),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = 0, y = -0.035, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
           xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
           text = "GDP per capita (PPP, 2021 international dollars, log scale)",
           font = list(size = 11, color = "#444444"))
    ),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Region"), orientation = "v",
                  x = 1.02, xanchor = "left", y = 1, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(l = 95, r = 150, t = 80, b = 130),
    hoverlabel = list(bgcolor = "white")
  ) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 700, transition = 300) |>
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE, scrollZoom = TRUE)
```

Three interactions earn their place here. The **animation** makes the upward
movement of the curve a thing you watch rather than a number you are told.
The **legend** switches regions on and off, which separates the question "how
does income relate to life expectancy" from "is the Sub-Saharan African cluster
tight or is it scattered", and the answer is visibly not tight. The **hover
tooltips** name every country and report its life expectancy, GDP per capita,
population, region and income group, so any point in the cloud can be
identified and checked. Bubble area is proportional to population, so the
reader can see that the countries that matter for most of the world's people are
not the ones sitting furthest from the line.

## 4. The pandemic interrupted the pattern

Between 2019 and 2021 life expectancy fell in almost every country in the world,
and the interruption was not spread evenly across income levels. Comparing what
happened against each country's own pre-pandemic pace isolates the break.

```{r}
#| label: covid-table
covid |>
  mutate(income_group = factor(income_group,
                               levels = c("Low", "Lower-middle", "Upper-middle", "High"))) |>
  arrange(income_group) |>
  transmute(
    `Income group` = income_group,
    n = n,
    `2010–2019 (yr/yr)` = sprintf("%+.2f", med_pre_pace),
    `2019–2021 (yr/yr)` = sprintf("%+.2f", med_covid_pace),
    `Behind trend` = sprintf("%.2f years", med_excess)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrcrr")
```

Life expectancy was rising in every income group before the pandemic and fell
in every income group during it. The upper-middle group lost the most —
`r num(abs(grp("Upper-middle", "med_excess")))` years against its own trend —
and the loss is concentrated: Paraguay, South Africa, Botswana, Peru, Ecuador
and Mexico each lost four to six years. High-income countries lost least, and
the ones that lost almost nothing are the ones with the lowest COVID mortality
and the slowest pre-pandemic pace: Australia, New Zealand, Norway, Japan.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income/main/results/fig2_covid_by_income.png)

The comparison uses medians rather than means on purpose. In a group of 21
low-income countries, one country in a mortality crisis — the Central African
Republic — moves the mean a long way, and it moves it in the wrong direction:
the mean low-income loss would read `r num(abs(grp("Low", "mean_excess")))`
years instead of `r num(abs(grp("Low", "med_excess")))`.

## 5. Who is above and below the curve

Residuals are taken from a pooled regression with year fixed effects, so each
country is compared with what other countries were achieving in the same year
rather than with a global average that ignores the curve's own movement. The
twelve largest positive and negative residuals over 1990–2023 are in
`results/outliers.csv`; the largest gaps are Albania
(`r num(outliers$mean_resid[1])` years), West Bank and Gaza
(`r num(outliers$mean_resid[2])` years) and China
(`r num(outliers$mean_resid[3])` years) on one side, and Nigeria
(`r num(abs(outliers$mean_resid[nrow(outliers)]))` years), Eswatini
(`r num(abs(outliers$mean_resid[nrow(outliers) - 1]))` years) and Equatorial
Guinea on the other. Every one of the twelve countries below the curve is in
Sub-Saharan Africa.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income/main/results/fig3_outliers.png)

Income is not the same thing as health. A country can be healthy for reasons
that are not in its income — a strong public health system, a diet, a low
violence rate — and that is visible in the residuals, which are large, stable
over three decades, and concentrated in a handful of countries with recognizable
stories behind them.

## 6. Spotlighting a single country

The animation answers "how did the curve move". The figure below answers the
complementary question: how did *individual countries* move? Every country is
drawn as a thin grey line that can be hovered, the seven regional medians are
highlighted and can be switched on and off in the legend, and the menu
spotlights one country against the backdrop of all the others. Switch it to
China or Nigeria and the difference in starting point, slope and pandemic dip
is immediate in a way that no table conveys.

```{r}
#| label: interactive-trajectories
#| fig-height: 6.6

all_lines <- panel |>
  arrange(country_iso3, year) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("<b>", country_name, "</b><br>Year: ", year,
                        "<br>Life expectancy: ", round(life_expectancy, 1), " years"))

regional_medians <- panel |>
  left_join(region_table, by = "region") |>
  group_by(region, region_short, year) |>
  summarise(median_life = median(life_expectancy), .groups = "drop")

# The menu offers the countries the analysis flagged as interesting, plus a
# spread of large economies, so it stays usable.
spotlight <- sort(unique(c(
  outliers$country_name,
  c("China", "India", "United States", "Brazil", "Nigeria", "Japan", "Germany",
    "Russia", "Indonesia", "Mexico", "Bangladesh", "Ethiopia")
)))
spotlight <- spotlight[spotlight %in% panel$country_name]

n_regions    <- nrow(region_table)
n_countries  <- length(spotlight)
total_traces <- 1 + n_regions + n_countries

# The dropdown is built from a visibility vector over the traces:
# 1 = all countries, 2..(1+n_regions) = the regional medians, the rest = one
# trace per spotlit country.
make_visible <- function(country) {
  vis <- rep("legendonly", total_traces)
  vis[1] <- "true"
  vis[2:(1 + n_regions)] <- "true"
  vis[1 + n_regions + match(country, spotlight)] <- "true"
  vis
}

p5 <- plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = all_lines, x = ~year, y = ~life_expectancy, text = ~label, hoverinfo = "text",
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#c9c9c9", width = 0.6),
    showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE
  )

for (i in seq_len(n_regions)) {
  p5 <- p5 |>
    add_trace(
      data = regional_medians |> filter(region == region_table$region[i]),
      x = ~year, y = ~median_life, name = region_table$region_short[i],
      type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
      line = list(width = 2.6, color = region_table$color[i]),
      hoverinfo = "y", inherit = FALSE
    )
}

for (cc in spotlight) {
  p5 <- p5 |>
    add_trace(
      data = panel |> filter(country_name == cc),
      x = ~year, y = ~life_expectancy,
      name = cc, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
      line = list(color = "#d6336c", width = 2.2),
      hoverinfo = "x+y", showlegend = FALSE,
      visible = if (cc == spotlight[1]) "true" else "legendonly",
      inherit = FALSE
    )
}

p5 |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Year", dtick = 5),
    yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy at birth (years)", range = c(35, 90)),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = 0, y = 1.20, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           showarrow = FALSE, text = "<b>Life expectancy trajectories, 1990–2023</b>",
           font = list(size = 16)),
      list(x = 0, y = 1.13, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           showarrow = FALSE, align = "left",
           text = "Every country is a thin grey line. Use the menu to spotlight one of them.",
           font = list(size = 11, color = "#666666"))
    ),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Regional median"), orientation = "v",
                  x = 1.02, xanchor = "left", y = 1, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(l = 70, r = 190, t = 150, b = 60),
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type = "dropdown", direction = "down", x = 0, y = 1.06, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
      active = 0,
      buttons = lapply(spotlight, function(cc) {
        list(label = cc, method = "restyle", args = list(list(visible = make_visible(cc))))
      })
    ))
  ) |>
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
```

## Robustness

Seven of the `r format(nrow(panel), big.mark = ",")` country-year observations
are acute mortality crises rather than informative points on the
income–health relation: Rwanda in 1994 (12.2 years of life), Somalia in
1991–93, and the Central African Republic in 2009, 2019 and 2022. They are
genuine observations and they stay in the main analysis, but the headline
numbers were re-estimated without them. The median slope moves from
`r num(sens$median_slope[1])` to `r num(sens$median_slope[2])`, the shift at
\$5,000 from `r num(sens$shift_5k_to_2019[1])` to
`r num(sens$shift_5k_to_2019[2])` years, and the pandemic losses are unchanged
to two decimals. The conclusions do not depend on the crisis years.

## Limitations

- **The curve is cross-sectional.** It describes what countries at a given
  income achieve, not what happens to a country when its income changes, so it
  is not a causal return on income.
- **Life expectancy is a population average.** It says nothing about inequality
  within a country.
- **Income groups are the current classification applied to all years**, so a
  country that moved between groups is counted in its present group throughout.
- **The pandemic window is short.** Some of the 2021 "excess loss" is
  catch-up rather than permanent loss, and a longer window would spread the
  same total over more years.

## Takeaway

Income buys life, and the price has been remarkably stable: about
`r num(ks("median_slope_by_year"))` years per doubling, every year, for thirty
years. The interesting part is what happens around that price. The curve has
been drifting upward underneath it — faster at the bottom, so a poor country
gained about `r num(ks("shift_5k_1990_to_2019"))` years between 1990 and 2019
where a rich one gained `r num(ks("shift_40k_1990_to_2019"))` — which is what
it looks like when public health technology improves faster than income grows.
And then the pandemic took it all back for two years, everywhere, with the
middle-income countries losing the most against their own trend.

None of this says that income stops mattering. The slope is still about 4.7
years per doubling. What the analysis adds is the size of the residuals: some
countries live many years more, and some many years less, than their income
predicts. Income is the price of health, but it is not the whole bill.

*Code and data: [github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income](https://github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog7-health-income). Data source: World Bank Indicators (CC BY 4.0).*
